title: The domestic church (CCC 1655–1658)
hookLine: the family home as a little church

lines: GRACE, FAST, BEFORE IT GETS COLD.
A KITCHEN TABLE ON A WEEKNIGHT.
cards: Someone says grace, fast, before the food goes cold. It's a weeknight: homework at one end of the kitchen table, a laptop at the other, a pot on the stove. A toddler joins in late with the amen.

On a shelf above the sink there's a small crucifix, a palm leaf from last spring gone brown, and a photo of a grandmother who died. It doesn't look like a holy room. The Catechism gives it a holy name all the same.

teach.b: The Catechism starts in the Acts of the Apostles, where more than once someone comes to believe together with their whole household.
The jailer at Philippi, shaken by an earthquake, is baptized that same night with all his family. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, is baptized with her household.
Paul and Silas tell the jailer that if he believes in the Lord Jesus, he and his house will be saved: the promise is made to a household.
These homes, the Catechism says, became islands of Christian life in a world that didn't yet believe. Then it takes a phrase from the Second Vatican Council: the family as the domestic church.

Ecclesia domestica. Not a metaphor for something lesser. The home is where children first hear the faith, from their parents, by word and example, and where a vocation, any vocation, is first noticed.

teach.h: THE FIRST SCHOOL OF CHRISTIAN LIFE.
teach.b: The Catechism calls it the first school of Christian life. There you learn endurance and the joy of work, love between brothers and sisters, and generous forgiveness, again and again.
There the family prays together and offers its life to God. So the ordinary things count: grace before meals, a blessing at bedtime, a fight made up before sleep.
And the Catechism doesn't forget people without a family nearby: the single, the widowed, people far from home. The Church's doors must be open to them, it says.
No one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone, especially those who labor and are burdened.

how: Catholic families may say grace before meals, pray at bedtime with children, keep a crucifix or holy images at home, and mark feasts and seasons such as Advent and Lent around the table.

a chapel built inside a private house
the family home as a little church

the jailer at Philippi and Lydia were baptized with their households.
the Catechism says only people with families belong to a domestic church

games.q: you live alone, far from family, and you hear the phrase domestic church. where does the Catechism say you belong?
o: the Church is a home and family for everyone.
games.why: the Catechism says the Church's doors must be open to people without families nearby: no one is without a family in this world.

practice: Think of who you share a home with, a partner, a child, a parent, a roommate, or no one right now, and picture one small moment when you could pause together: before a meal, at bedtime, on a phone call if you live apart.
If you pray, that could be an Our Father or grace before eating; if you don't, a moment of quiet thanks at the table does the same work of noticing.

wordCard.voice: Domestic church. The home as a little church: the household where faith is first heard, prayed and practiced, with the Church's doors open to everyone without one. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the church of the home.

carryVoice: Your line: a little church. It can be a kitchen table. Go gently.
